tagline: Mountain waters, a power-company lake and a gap shared by railroads
intro: Mountain Maryland runs from Keysers Ridge to Cumberland on state routes and country roads through forested highlands. Maryland’s tourism office gives the branched scenic byway 193 miles and five to seven hours of driving. Its description emphasizes forests, rivers and four-season recreation, from hiking and skiing to fishing and boating. The opening ridge stands at 2,894 feet; farther on, the route reaches lake country and the mountain gap west of Cumberland.

Travel and industry reshaped the landscapes this corridor now joins. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad helped Deer Park grow as a mountain resort; when automobiles freed travelers from rail service, its appeal declined. Deep Creek Lake came from a different enterprise: a hydroelectric project whose dam was built between 1923 and 1925. Maryland bought the lake in 2000, and Deep Creek Lake State Park provides public access.

From Keysers Ridge, the western approach goes toward Friendsville before turning south to McHenry, Deep Creek Lake and Oakland. At Oakland the byway branches toward the Allegheny Highlands, Kitzmiller and Savage River State Forest. Continue north through Lonaconing and Frostburg toward Cumberland, where roads and railways share the Narrows with Wills Creek. The final landmark is the water gap between Wills Mountain and Haystack Mountain.

moments.title: Cranesville Swamp
moments.text: Cranesville Swamp occupies a natural bowl that creates a climate more like regions farther north. The preserve straddles Garrett County, Maryland, and Preston County, West Virginia. Its 19 plant communities include sphagnum moss, sedges and speckled alder, with round-leaved sundew among the bog plants. It also holds the southernmost natural community of American larches. The Nature Conservancy began acquiring the preserve in 1960; National Natural Landmark designation followed in 1964. The northern water shrew has been documented here, along with bird records for the golden-crowned kinglet and Nashville warbler, species rarely seen in this area.

moments.title: Swallow Falls
moments.text: The 53-foot drop of Muddy Creek Falls shares this park with old hemlocks, some more than 300 years old. Swallow Falls lies on the west bank of the Youghiogheny River, northwest of Oakland. Its public-land history began in 1906, when John and Robert Garrett donated 1,917 acres for a state forest. That land included the future Swallow Falls and Herrington Manor parks, both developed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s. Smaller waterfalls also descend along the Youghiogheny and Tolivar Creek. Thomas Edison, Henry Ford, John Burroughs and Harvey Firestone camped at Muddy Creek Falls during the summers of 1918 and 1921.
moments.notice: Muddy Creek Falls drops 53 feet; smaller falls lie on the Youghiogheny River and Tolivar Creek.

moments.title: Cumberland Narrows
moments.text: Wills Creek cuts a low passage between Wills Mountain and Haystack Mountain, with quartzite cliffs and fallen rock prominent in the gap. Travel routes share that opening: Nemacolin’s Path became the Old National Road, now Alternate US 40. The former B&O main line is part of CSX, while a former Western Maryland Railway line carries scenic excursion trains and the Great Allegheny Passage bike trail. Lover’s Leap is the rocky outcrop on Wills Mountain’s northeast side of the Narrows. The passage serves as Cumberland’s western gateway to the Appalachian Plateau and the Ohio River Valley beyond.
